newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - US debt volatilities mixed after FOMC.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - US debt volatilities mixed after FOMC.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. fixed income options were narrowly mixed after a two-day Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting ended today without a credit tightening, dealers said.

"We still have the employment numbers on Friday," said a Eurodollar trader at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME). "I think people are very concerned about Friday's numbers, which should keep a cap on how much vols come off."
A Treasury bond option trader at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) agreed that the market had entered a pre-employment report standoff.
"Vols were bid early but probably came in just a little after the news," he said. "I don't expect much from here until the payroll numbers."

T-bond futures saw a moderate sell-off after the FOMC news in mid-afternoon. But volatilities did not spike up in response as the market viewed the decline as caused mainly by profit-taking after recent rallies, traders said.
Implied volatility for March T-bond futures options finished at 10.0 percent, marginally below Tuesday's close. Option volume was moderate with several trades of 1,000 to 2,000 contracts.

In one of the largest trades, an investment bank bought about 2,000 contracts of deep-out-of-the-money June 120 calls, which had seen volume of almost 6,000 contracts on Tuesday. A large number of June 124 calls were also said to have traded.

While it was not unusual for speculators to make cheap speculative bets by buying large lots of low-delta options prior to an important economic indicator, traders were puzzled by the seemingly unrealistic strike prices.
In the CME Eurodollar pit, implied volatilities for June and September options were little changed at 10.8 and 14.2 percent respectively.
Traders said Eurodollar volatilities have been floundering at historically low levels and had little room to fall, at least for now until the jobs data.

"To this point, vols are very, very cheap," the CME trader said, noting that the market had only partially priced in a Federal Reserve rate hike even though many economists still expected tighter credit later in the year.
"But if we are in a 5.5-percent-LIBOR-forever scenario or the Fed's on hold for another year, they will get cheaper," the trader said of volatilities.
